content: Parts of the human digestive system: mouth, salivary glands, esophagus, stomach, liver, pancreas, gallbladder, small intestine, large intestine, and anus. These are the parts of our digestive system.

The food enters the digestive system through the mouth and then passes down into the stomach through the esophagus. From the stomach it passes to the small intestine, from there to the large intestine, and the undigested food is finally excreted through the anus. This is the flow of food in our digestive system.

All these parts are connected to one another and form a long tube or canal called the alimentary canal. Glands like salivary glands, liver, gallbladder, and pancreas are attached to the alimentary canal and form the digestive system. Accessory glands plus alimentary canal together make the digestive system.

Digestion begins in the mouth. Whatever food we eat should be made soft and wet before swallowing, because if it is rough and dry it cannot easily travel through the alimentary canal. The teeth, saliva, and tongue do this job. Teeth break the food into smaller pieces, saliva makes the food wet, and the tongue mixes the food with saliva to form a bolus.

Saliva is a liquid secreted by three pairs of salivary glands present in our mouth. Saliva has an enzyme called salivary amylase or ptyalin. It digests carbohydrates like starch into sugars. The bolus then has to travel throughout the alimentary canal.

The muscles of the alimentary canal produce rhythmic contractions and relaxations. These contractions and relaxations create a wave-like movement called peristaltic movements. These peristaltic movements help the food move throughout the alimentary canal.

Food from the mouth enters the stomach through the esophagus. The stomach is a bag-like organ that expands when food enters it. The walls of the stomach have gastric glands. These gastric glands secrete HCl, pepsin, and mucus.

HCl, hydrochloric acid, kills bacteria that enter the stomach along with food. HCl also makes the pH of the stomach acidic because proteins need an acidic medium for digestion. Pepsin is a digestive enzyme which digests proteins. Mucus protects the walls of the stomach from the action of hydrochloric acid.

The food that is partly digested in the stomach turns into a semi-solid paste called chyme. This chyme is released into the small intestine part by part by a sphincter muscle called the pyloric sphincter.

The small intestine is a long coiled tube. It is highly coiled to fit in a small space. The small intestine receives bile juice from the liver, pancreatic juice from the pancreas, and intestinal juice from the walls of the small intestine. Pancreatic and intestinal juices contain enzymes like trypsin, lipase, pancreatic amylase, peptidases, and nucleases.

Bile does not contain any enzymes, but it does two important things. First, it breaks fat globules into smaller globules so the action of enzymes on fats becomes easy. Second, it changes the pH of the intestine to alkaline because digestion of fats and carbohydrates takes place in alkaline medium.

In the small intestine, enzymes like pancreatic amylase, sucrase, maltase, and lactase digest carbohydrates to simple sugars such as glucose, galactose, and fructose. Enzymes like trypsin, chymotrypsin, and peptidases convert proteins and peptides into amino acids. Lipase converts fats into fatty acids and glycerol.

The nutrients from the digested food are absorbed into the walls of the small intestine. The inner lining of the small intestine has finger-like projections called villi. Each villus is richly supplied with blood vessels and lymph vessels. The digested nutrients are absorbed into the villi and supplied to different parts of the body.

The undigested food passes into the large intestine. Here water is absorbed into the blood and the remaining solid waste becomes faeces and is finally excreted out through the anus. This is the human digestive system.
